notes: "The sea got the old king's name." is a little flat; "The sea took the old king's name." or simply dropping it before "People call it the Aegean Sea." would read more naturally.
Condensed version omits Ariadne leaving with Theseus and Naxos; acceptable simplification for A1.
"White sails can tell me the good news from far away." is slightly stiff; "When I see white sails, I know the good news." stays within present simple and reads more naturally.
Ariadne disappears from the story after the Labyrinth (no flight/Naxos); acceptable condensing, but a short line such as "Ariadne went with them." would avoid a reader wondering where she went.
"Each of them liked to trouble strangers on the lonely mountain paths." -- 'trouble' is a bit mild/vague; "liked to attack strangers" or "played cruel tricks on strangers" is clearer.
No conditionals or passives found; relative clause 'a dark maze that Daedalus made for him' is fine at B1.
Softening of Androgeus's death ('had died while visiting Athens') and Ariadne 'stayed behind' on Naxos are acceptable child-friendly condensations of the myth.

Two consecutive paragraphs open their key action with 'That night' ('That night she crept...' / 'That night Theseus went into the Labyrinth'); varying one (e.g. 'Before the palace stirred, Theseus went into the Labyrinth') would read better.
"each year Athens must send" in past narrative is literary and acceptable; "had to send" would be the more neutral alternative.

summary: All five levels retell the Theseus myth faithfully (stone and tokens, road robbers, recognition by the sword at the feast, tribute, Ariadne's thread, victory, Naxos, forgotten white sails, Aegeus's death and the naming of the Aegean) with no film-derived elements. Grammar stays within level limits, quizzes have single correct keyed answers, and violence and deaths are stated, never depicted, so the text suits a 4+ rating. Only minor stylistic notes remain.
